metadata.narrative: Our city council is considering a local child allowance or refundable child tax credit for families with low incomes, but some members want to put the money into job programs, TANF-style work requirements, or an EITC expansion instead. Can you help me understand what the evidence says about monthly cash for families with children? How should we weigh poverty reduction, food and housing hardship, parents’ work incentives, racial equity, children’s long-term mobility, and administrative pitfalls if we want a policy that is practical for a mid-sized city?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Understanding what monthly cash for families with children does, compared with job programs, TANF-style work mandates, and EITC expansion, requires looking separately at poverty, hardship, work incentives, equity, mobility, and administration.

On poverty reduction, Columbia researchers found that paying the 2021 expanded Child Tax Credit monthly rather than as an annual lump sum kept roughly a third more children out of poverty in any given month by smoothing the income volatility that pushes families below the line between paychecks.
By December 2021 the expansion had cut child poverty by about 29 percent, roughly 3 million fewer children, and economists estimate the effect would have been larger still with full take-up.

Take-up is a real constraint: nearly 29 percent of eligible low- and moderate-income families knew little about the credit, and non-filers without internet access struggled to register through the IRS portal.
On food and housing hardship, the same monthly payments cut food insufficiency by about a quarter within six weeks, with the largest gains among Black and Hispanic families.
A National Academies-cited analysis found the CTC expansion reduced poverty, food insecurity, and material hardship without reducing parental employment.
EITC income has separately been linked to a 15 percent overall reduction in severe housing cost burden among eligible households, rising to 31 percent for families with two children.

On racial equity, the 2021 CTC's outsized benefit to Black and Latino children came specifically from dropping the earnings requirement that had excluded the lowest-income families, cutting Black child poverty by 8.8 points and Latino child poverty by 6.3 points.

Reverting to the earnings-linked design denies the full credit to 45 percent of Black children and 39 percent of Latino children, showing how work-conditioning a credit reproduces labor-market discrimination.
An EITC-based approach carries its own equity risk, since EITC claimants face disproportionately higher IRS audit rates, with documented disparities affecting Black taxpayers.
More broadly, the "deserving versus undeserving poor" distinction underlying work-conditioned benefits has racially coded historical roots.
On work incentives, the record cuts against a simple "cash discourages work" story.
The federal EITC has a strong record of pulling single mothers into the labor force, and the 2021 CTC did not reduce parental employment despite having no work test at all.
Stockton's SEED pilot reinforces this: full-time employment among $500-per-month recipients rose from 28 percent to 40 percent over the first year.

By contrast, rigorous evaluations of thirteen mandatory welfare-to-work programs found employment gains faded by year five, with most recipients working regardless of the mandate, and only two programs meaningfully reduced poverty.

After 1996 TANF work requirements took effect, deep poverty among female-headed families more than doubled, because mothers who could not meet work mandates lost cash assistance with no remaining safety net.
Even the celebrated 1990s employment gains among single mothers are better attributed to the concurrent EITC expansion and a booming economy than to the work requirements themselves.

On children's long-term mobility, a randomized trial called Baby's First Years found that mothers given $333 monthly, unconditional cash had one-year-olds with measurably different brain activity linked to later language and cognitive skills, compared to mothers given a nominal $20.
Complementing this, a $3,000 annual income increase before age six is associated with a child's future work hours rising by 135 per year and earnings by 17 percent between ages 25 and 37.
On administrative pitfalls, the central problem for a city is stacked benefit phase-outs.

Combining SNAP, EITC, and housing assistance can push effective marginal tax rates from roughly 30 percent to 55 percent, and as high as 82 percent at the top of the phase-out range, a pattern researchers call a "twice poverty trap."
The Congressional Budget Office similarly calculates an average 31 percent marginal tax rate once payroll and income taxes combine with SNAP and refundable-credit phase-outs.

One economist argues work requirements function as an imperfect substitute for the incentive lost to these stacked phase-outs, and suggests time-limited rather than income-limited benefits as an alternative.

A separate review recommends basing eligibility on the child's needs rather than a parent's work status, and streamlining overlapping applications so families are not filing separately for each program.

On practicality for a mid-sized city, Stockton's SEED program and comparable efforts in other cities demonstrate that municipal cash pilots are administratively feasible, often funded through a mix of philanthropy and city funds, with national mayoral associations now offering formal design guidance.

Weighing this evidence, a monthly child allowance reaching families regardless of earnings does the most reliable work on poverty, hardship, and racial equity, without evidence that it discourages parental work.
An EITC expansion is a valuable complement with its own strong employment record, but by design it cannot reach jobless households, which are often in the deepest poverty.
TANF-style work mandates carry the weakest evidence of net poverty reduction and the clearest risk of pushing vulnerable families into deeper poverty.
The most defensible city design pairs a near-unconditional monthly child benefit with simplified eligibility and coordinated phase-outs to avoid recreating a local benefits cliff.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

output.text:
The evidence base on cash assistance for families with children versus job programs, TANF-style work mandates, and EITC expansion is now large enough to give the council a clear, if nuanced, picture.

On poverty reduction, the 2021 expanded Child Tax Credit is the best-documented natural experiment: Columbia University researchers found that paying the credit monthly rather than as an annual lump sum kept roughly a third more children out of poverty in any given month, because monthly payments smooth the income volatility that pushes families below the poverty line between paydays.
By December 2021 the expansion had cut child poverty by about 29 percent, translating into roughly 3 million fewer children in poverty, and economists estimate the effect would have been even larger with full take-up.
Take-up matters because nearly 29 percent of low- and moderate-income families surveyed knew little or nothing about the credit, and non-filers without internet access struggled to register through the IRS portal, a concrete administrative pitfall for any locally run program.

On food and housing hardship, the same monthly CTC payments cut food insufficiency by about a quarter within six weeks of the first checks, with the largest gains among Black and Hispanic families.
Separately, a National Academies-cited analysis found the CTC expansion reduced poverty, food insecurity, and material hardship without reducing parental employment, directly undercutting the assumption that unconditional cash discourages work.
On the EITC side, additional earned income has been linked to a 15 percent overall reduction in severe housing cost burden among eligible households, rising to 31 percent for families with two children, showing that work-conditioned credits also relieve housing hardship, just for a narrower population of working families.

On racial equity, the 2021 CTC's disproportionate benefit to Black and Latino children came specifically because it dropped the earnings requirement that had excluded families with little or no income, cutting Black child poverty by 8.8 percentage points and Latino child poverty by 6.3 points.
Reverting to the non-refundable, earnings-linked design denies the full credit to 45 percent of Black children, 39 percent of Latino children, and 38 percent of American Indian and Alaska Native children, illustrating how work-conditioning a credit reproduces racial gaps rooted in labor-market discrimination.
The EITC alternative carries its own equity cost: EITC claimants face disproportionately higher IRS audit rates, with documented racial disparities affecting Black taxpayers, an administrative burden a city-run EITC supplement would need to anticipate if state or federal audit risk is inherited by recipients.
Historically, the very distinction between "deserving" and "undeserving" poor that underlies work requirements has roots in racially coded assumptions about who merits unconditional help.

On work incentives, the record is mixed by design rather than by ideology.
The federal EITC has a strong, well-replicated record of pulling single mothers into the labor force, an effect economists attribute to more than half of the 1984–1996 rise in single-mother employment, and the 2021 CTC itself did not reduce parental employment despite lacking any work test.
Stockton's SEED guaranteed-income pilot reinforces this: full-time employment among $500-per-month recipients rose from 28 percent to 40 percent over the first year, weakening the standard critique that unconditional cash reduces work effort.
By contrast, rigorous evaluations of mandatory welfare-to-work programs found employment gains faded by the fifth year, with at least three-quarters of recipients working regardless of whether they faced a mandate, and only two of thirteen studied programs meaningfully reduced poverty.
Historical TANF data show something more troubling for a "job programs instead of cash" strategy: after the 1996 work requirements took effect, deep poverty among female-headed families more than doubled, because many mothers who could not meet work mandates lost cash assistance with no safety net left to catch them.
Even the celebrated 1990s employment gains among single mothers are better attributed to the concurrent EITC expansion and a booming economy than to work requirements themselves, since the EITC expansion alone had a larger measured effect on work than the welfare law changes.

On children's long-term mobility, a randomized controlled trial called Baby's First Years found that mothers randomly assigned $333 monthly, unconditional cash showed measurable differences in their one-year-olds' brain activity linked to later language, cognitive, and school-readiness skills, compared to mothers receiving a nominal $20.
Complementing this, research on EITC- and CTC-style income finds that a $3,000 annual income increase before age six raises a child's future work hours by 135 per year and earnings by 17 percent between ages 25 and 37, alongside improved test scores and higher college attendance.

On administrative pitfalls, the central problem a mid-sized city must solve is stacked benefit phase-outs.
When SNAP, EITC, TANF-linked supports, and housing assistance are combined, effective marginal tax rates can climb from roughly 30 percent to 55 percent and, at the highest phase-out ranges, 82 percent, a pattern researchers call a "twice poverty trap" because it strikes hardest just above the poverty line.
The Congressional Budget Office similarly calculates an average 31 percent marginal tax rate for low- and moderate-income workers once payroll taxes, income taxes, and benefit phase-outs from SNAP and refundable credits are combined.
One economist argues that mandatory work requirements exist precisely as an imperfect substitute for the incentive lost to these stacked phase-outs, and proposes alternatives such as time-limited rather than income-limited benefits or consumption-based eligibility tests to reduce the disincentive without abandoning means-testing entirely.
A separate policy review recommends easing this complexity by basing eligibility on the child's needs rather than a parent's work or immigration status, and by streamlining overlapping applications and recertification across programs so families are not required to repeat paperwork four separate times to keep four separate benefits.

On practicality for a mid-sized city specifically, Stockton's SEED program and comparable efforts in Compton, Los Angeles, and Newark demonstrate that city-scale monthly cash pilots are administratively feasible, often financed through a mix of private philanthropy and municipal funds, with the National League of Cities and U.S. Conference of Mayors now offering formal guidance for local guaranteed-income design.

Weighing all of this, a monthly child allowance structured to reach families regardless of earnings appears to do the most reliable work on poverty, hardship, and racial equity, and the strongest available evidence does not show it discourages parental work.
An EITC expansion is a valuable complement for working families and has its own long track record on employment, health, and schooling, but by design it cannot reach jobless households, which are often the deepest in poverty.
TANF-style work mandates carry the weakest evidence of net poverty reduction and the clearest risk of pushing the most vulnerable families into deeper poverty, making them a poor substitute for direct cash if the council's central goal is protecting children.
The most defensible city design, based on this evidence, pairs a near-unconditional monthly child benefit with simplified, non-duplicative eligibility rules and coordinated phase-outs to avoid recreating a local benefits cliff.
